title: Maternal and Child Health Literacy
subtitle: Recognise danger signs in pregnancy, newborns and young children, plan ahead, and get the right care without delay.
description: A practical course, based on World Health Organization guidance, on antenatal and postnatal care, birth planning, newborn and child danger signs, and the prevention habits that protect children. You finish with a family health action plan and a 90-day plan to share what you learned. This course builds health literacy only: it does not replace care from a health worker and never gives medicine doses.
outcomes: Name the danger signs in pregnancy, after birth, in newborns and in sick children, and act on them immediately
Plan all eight WHO antenatal contacts and the postnatal checks from real dates
Write a birth and emergency plan with transport, decision makers and a weekly saving target
Respond safely at home to diarrhoea, fever and cough while getting a health worker's help
Keep vaccination cards, nets and hygiene habits on track using a household checklist
Share checked health information kindly and run a measurable 90-day outreach plan
audience: Women and caregivers, pregnant or not, who want to protect mothers and children in their family and community, with no medical background needed.
tools: A smartphone with a calendar app, or a notebook and pen
Antenatal card or child vaccination card, if you have one
Phone numbers of your nearest health facilities
Two ORS sachets for the sick-child kit

modules.title: Foundations: Pregnancy Care and Danger Signs
modules.overview: Why mothers and newborns die and what prevents it, how the WHO eight-contact antenatal schedule works, and the danger signs that mean a woman must go to a facility now. Every lesson ends with a practical task you can do at home.

lessons.title: Why mothers and newborns die, and what prevents it
objectives: Name the five complications behind most maternal deaths, according to WHO
Explain why the first week of life is the riskiest time for a newborn
Describe the three places where time is lost between a danger sign and treatment
State clearly what this course can and cannot do for you

blocks.text: This course is about one practical skill: **knowing when a pregnant woman, a new mother, a newborn or a young child needs a health worker, and getting them there in time**. It is not a medical course. It will not teach you to diagnose or treat anyone, and it never gives medicine doses. What it gives you is health literacy: the ability to understand health information, recognise danger, ask good questions at the clinic and act quickly.

blocks.title: This course does not replace a health worker
blocks.text: Everything here supports, and never replaces, care from a trained health worker at a clinic, primary health care centre or hospital. If you see a danger sign, do not wait to finish a lesson or to ask friends on WhatsApp. Go to a health facility.
What the World Health Organization tells us

The World Health Organization (WHO) publishes fact sheets on maternal and newborn deaths. Its maternal mortality fact sheet estimates that about **260,000 women died in 2023** from causes linked to pregnancy and childbirth. That is **over 700 women every day**, and about **92% of these deaths happened in low and lower-middle income countries**. WHO also says plainly that **most maternal deaths are preventable**, because the health care solutions are well known.
According to WHO, five complications account for about **75% of all maternal deaths**:

head: Complication
What it means in plain words
What families can watch for
rows: Severe bleeding
Heavy bleeding, mostly after the baby is born
Bleeding that soaks cloths or pads quickly, feeling faint
Infections
Usually after childbirth
Fever, feeling very unwell, bad smelling discharge
High blood pressure (pre-eclampsia and eclampsia)
Blood pressure becomes dangerously high in pregnancy; eclampsia means fits
Severe headache, blurred vision, pain high in the belly, fits
Complications from delivery
Problems during labour and birth
Labour that is not progressing, any emergency during birth
Unsafe abortion
Abortion done by untrained people or in unsafe conditions
Bleeding, fever or severe pain afterwards

blocks.name: pregnant-woman
blocks.caption: Most pregnancy deaths come from a small number of complications that skilled care can manage.

blocks.text: Newborns: the first week matters most

WHO's newborn mortality fact sheet reports that **2.3 million newborns died in their first 28 days in 2022**, and that **about 75% of newborn deaths happen in the first week of life**. Sub-Saharan Africa has the highest newborn death rate in the world, at about 27 deaths per 1,000 live births. The main causes are being born too early, problems during birth (such as the baby not breathing well), infections and birth defects.

This is why the hours and days right after birth get so much attention in this course. A baby who stops feeding well, becomes floppy, breathes with difficulty, has a fever, has fits or feels cold needs care quickly.
Where time is lost
When a woman or child dies from a complication that could have been treated, time has usually been lost somewhere along the way. It helps to think of three places where this happens:

blocks.title: Three places time is lost
items: Danger sign appears
Delay deciding at home
Delay on the road
Delay at the facility
Treatment
blocks.caption: Health literacy shortens the first delay, and planning shortens the second.

items: **Deciding at home.** Nobody recognises the danger sign, or the family waits for a husband, mother-in-law or pastor to give permission, or tries home remedies first.
**Getting there.** There is no transport at night, no money for the fare, or nobody knows which facility can handle the problem.
**At the facility.** The facility lacks staff, blood or supplies, or the woman arrives without her records and the staff must start from zero.

blocks.text: You cannot fix every problem at the facility, but you can do a lot about the first two. Knowing the danger signs removes the first delay. A written plan for transport, money and the right facility removes much of the second. Carrying the antenatal card or child health card helps with the third.

blocks.title: Worked example: finding the delays in a real-life story
blocks.context: For example, Ngozi is 34 weeks pregnant and lives about 40 minutes by road from the general hospital. One evening she has a severe headache and says her eyes are blurry.
steps: Her sister says it is probably tiredness and suggests she sleeps. This is a possible **delay at home**: a severe headache with blurred vision is a warning sign of pre-eclampsia.
Her husband is travelling, and she does not want to go without his permission. Another **delay at home**.
At 10 pm they look for a car. The usual driver is not answering. This is a **delay on the road**.
They finally arrive at midnight, without her antenatal card. Staff must ask many questions before they can see her history. This adds a **delay at the facility**.
blocks.result: Each delay was avoidable: knowing the sign, agreeing in advance that she can go without waiting for permission, saving a second driver's number, and keeping the card in her bag. These are exactly the habits this course builds.

blocks.text: What you will learn

items: The WHO schedule of eight antenatal contacts, and what to expect at each.
Danger signs in pregnancy, after birth, in newborns and in sick children.
How to make a birth and emergency plan, including transport and money.
Postnatal checks, prevention habits such as vaccines and mosquito nets, and simple home care while you get help.
How to share accurate information in your family and community, and how to spot health myths.

blocks.title: About the numbers in this course
blocks.text: Global figures come from WHO fact sheets and are estimates. They help you see the size of the problem. They do not predict what will happen to any one woman or child.

takeaways: WHO says most maternal deaths are preventable.
Five complications, led by severe bleeding, cause about three quarters of maternal deaths.
The first week of life is the riskiest time for a newborn.
Time is lost at home, on the road and at the facility; knowledge and planning cut the first two.
This course supports care from a health worker; it never replaces it.

activity.title: Map your own delays
steps: Write the name of the facility you would go to tonight if a pregnant woman in your home had a danger sign.
Write how long it takes to get there and how you would travel at night.
Write who in your household could decide to go without waiting for anyone else.
Circle the weakest point in your answers. That is your first delay to fix.
activity.evidence: A short note or photo of your written answers, with the weakest point circled.

lessons.title: Antenatal care: the eight contacts and what happens at each
objectives: Explain the WHO recommendation of at least eight antenatal contacts
Plan the dates of all contacts from the week of the first visit
List the main checks and preventive care offered during antenatal care
Prepare questions and documents to take to each visit

blocks.text: **Antenatal care (ANC)** is the care a woman receives from a skilled health worker during pregnancy. In 2016 WHO updated its guidance and now recommends **a minimum of eight contacts** during pregnancy, instead of the older model of four visits. WHO says that moving to eight contacts can reduce deaths of babies around the time of birth and improve women's experience of care.
The word **contact** is used instead of visit because a contact means real, active interaction with a health worker, not just collecting a card or waiting in a queue.
The WHO timing

WHO recommends that the **first contact happens in the first 12 weeks of pregnancy**, with later contacts at **20, 26, 30, 34, 36, 38 and 40 weeks**. Notice that the contacts become closer together near the end, when problems such as high blood pressure are more likely to appear.

blocks.title: Eight antenatal contacts
items: First: by 12 weeks
20 and 26 weeks
30 and 34 weeks
36 and 38 weeks
40 weeks
blocks.caption: Contacts are spaced widely early on and every two weeks in the last month.

blocks.name: stethoscope
blocks.caption: At every contact the health worker checks the mother and the baby, not only fills a card.

blocks.text: What happens during antenatal care
The exact services depend on your facility, but WHO's antenatal care guidance includes these elements. Knowing them helps you notice if something was missed and ask about it politely.

head: What is offered
Why it matters
rows: Blood pressure check and urine test
To catch high blood pressure and protein in the urine, signs of pre-eclampsia
Daily iron and folic acid supplements
To prevent anaemia in the mother and problems for the baby. The health worker decides the product and amount.
One ultrasound scan before 24 weeks
To estimate how far along the pregnancy is and look for problems with the baby
Tetanus vaccination
To protect the newborn from tetanus
Malaria prevention
Preventive treatment in pregnancy (called IPTp) where malaria is common, and sleeping under a mosquito net
Questions about alcohol and other substances
So the health worker can give support and advice

blocks.title: Never self-prescribe in pregnancy
blocks.text: Only take medicines and supplements given or approved by your health worker. Do not buy pregnancy medicines on your own from a chemist or a hawker, and do not copy what a friend was given. This course will never tell you how much of any medicine to take.
Planning your dates

Many women start antenatal care late, sometimes after 20 weeks, because they feel well or because the clinic is far. The first contact in the first 12 weeks is important because it allows the dating scan to be planned in time, starts iron and folic acid early, and gives the health worker a baseline for blood pressure and weight.

blocks.title: Worked example: writing out all eight contact dates
blocks.context: For example, Halima had her first antenatal contact on Tuesday 3 March 2026, when the health worker told her she was 11 weeks pregnant. She wants all her contact dates in her phone calendar.
steps: Week 20 is 9 weeks after week 11. 9 weeks is 63 days. 3 March plus 63 days is **Tuesday 5 May 2026**.
Week 26 is 6 weeks later: **Tuesday 16 June 2026**.
Week 30 is 4 weeks later: **Tuesday 14 July 2026**. Week 34 is 4 weeks later: **Tuesday 11 August 2026**.
Weeks 36, 38 and 40 are every 2 weeks: **25 August, 8 September and 22 September 2026**.
She adds each date to her phone calendar with a reminder two days before, and writes them on the inside cover of her antenatal card.
blocks.result: Halima has seven more dates planned, making eight contacts in total. If the clinic gives her a different date, she follows the clinic, because the health worker may adjust the schedule for her situation.

blocks.text: Making each contact count

items: Take your antenatal card or booklet to every visit, and any scan or test results.
Write down questions before you go. For example: What was my blood pressure? Is my blood level okay? When is my next visit?
Tell the health worker about anything new: headaches, bleeding, fever, pain, swelling, or worries about the baby's movements.
Ask what your blood pressure and test results mean, and write them down.
Before leaving, confirm the date of your next contact.

blocks.text: Antenatal care is also where you get information about birth planning, breastfeeding and family planning after birth. If your partner or a family member can come with you to at least one visit, they will hear the same information and be better prepared to help.

Keep all your antenatal records together in one plastic sleeve or envelope: the card, scan reports and test results. Take a clear photo of each page on your phone after every contact. If the card is lost or you go to a different facility in an emergency, these photos help the staff understand your pregnancy quickly.

blocks.title: If you missed a visit
blocks.text: Go as soon as you can. Do not wait for the next scheduled date or feel ashamed to return. A late contact is far better than no contact.

takeaways: WHO recommends at least eight antenatal contacts.
The first contact should happen in the first 12 weeks.
Later contacts are at 20, 26, 30, 34, 36, 38 and 40 weeks.
Blood pressure checks, iron and folic acid, an early scan, tetanus vaccination and malaria prevention are part of good care.
Only take medicines and supplements from your health worker.

activity.title: Build your contact calendar
steps: Choose a real or example first-contact date and the week of pregnancy at that visit.
Calculate the date of each remaining contact (20, 26, 30, 34, 36, 38, 40 weeks).
Enter the dates into a phone calendar with reminders.
Write three questions you would ask at the next contact.
activity.evidence: A screenshot of the calendar or a written list of eight dates plus your three questions.

lessons.title: Danger signs in pregnancy and after birth
objectives: Recognise the warning signs of pre-eclampsia, severe bleeding and infection
Tell the difference between a common discomfort and a danger sign
Apply the rule: danger sign means go now, day or night
Explain the danger signs to another family member in simple words

blocks.text: Pregnancy brings many changes that are uncomfortable but usually normal, such as tiredness or mild nausea. A **danger sign** is different. It is a sign that something may be seriously wrong and that the woman needs a health worker **now**, not tomorrow and not after a home remedy. In this lesson we focus on the signs linked to the main causes of maternal death described by WHO.
High blood pressure: pre-eclampsia and eclampsia

WHO's pre-eclampsia fact sheet describes it as high blood pressure (140/90 or more) with protein in the urine, **after 20 weeks of pregnancy**. Without treatment it can lead to **eclampsia (fits)**, damage to the kidneys, liver and brain, separation of the placenta, early birth, and death of the mother or baby. The warning signs WHO lists are:

items: **Severe headache** that does not go away.
**Problems with vision**, such as blurred vision or seeing spots.
**Pain in the upper belly**.
**Fits (convulsions)**, which mean eclampsia and are an emergency.

blocks.text: WHO notes that the risk is higher in first pregnancies, twin or multiple pregnancies, women with obesity, and women who already have high blood pressure, diabetes or kidney disease. This is one reason blood pressure is checked at every antenatal contact.
Bleeding and infection

WHO identifies **severe bleeding, mostly after childbirth**, as a leading cause of maternal death, and **infections, usually after childbirth**, as another. So the danger signs continue after the baby is born. Heavy bleeding, fever, or feeling very unwell in the days after birth are reasons to go immediately.

blocks.name: warning-sign
blocks.caption: A danger sign is a signal to act now, not to wait and watch.

head: Sign
Common and usually normal
Danger: go now
rows: Headache
Mild headache that goes with rest and water
Severe headache that does not go away, especially with blurred vision, after 20 weeks
Belly pain
Mild aches or stretching feelings
Severe pain, or pain high in the belly
Bleeding
Not applicable: any bleeding should be reported to a health worker
Heavy bleeding at any time, during pregnancy or after birth
Temperature
Feeling warm in hot weather
Fever, chills or feeling very unwell, especially after birth
Fits
None are normal
Any fit or convulsion is an emergency

blocks.title: Discomfort or danger?
items: Watch and mention at next contact
Go to a facility now
left: Mild aches that ease with rest
blocks.caption: When you are unsure which side a sign belongs on, treat it as danger and go.

blocks.text: The rule: danger sign means go now

When a danger sign appears, the safest response is always the same: **go to a health facility that can handle emergencies, immediately, day or night**. Do not wait to see if it gets better. Do not give herbal mixtures or medicines bought on the way. Bring the antenatal card. If possible, call the facility on the way so they are ready.

Which facility? For a danger sign, choose a facility that can manage emergencies, such as a general hospital, rather than the nearest small health post, if both can be reached. A small health post may need to send the woman on to a hospital, which adds a second journey. Ask at your antenatal contact which hospital your clinic refers emergencies to, and write it on your danger sign card.

blocks.title: If a woman is having a fit
blocks.text: Keep her away from fire, water and sharp objects, lie her on her side once the fit allows, do not put anything in her mouth, and get her to a facility immediately. Eclampsia needs treatment that only a health facility can give.

blocks.title: Worked example: a phone call from a neighbour
blocks.context: For example, Blessing's neighbour Amaka, 30 weeks pregnant with her first baby, calls at 7 pm. She says she has had a bad headache since morning and her eyes feel blurry. She asks whether she should take paracetamol and lie down.
steps: Blessing checks the signs: severe headache that has lasted all day, blurred vision, after 20 weeks, first pregnancy. These match the WHO warning signs of pre-eclampsia.
She does not suggest any medicine. She says: "These are danger signs. You need your blood pressure checked tonight."
She asks Amaka who can take her and helps her call the driver on her emergency list.
She reminds her to bring her antenatal card and phone charger.
blocks.result: Amaka reaches the hospital within the hour, where her blood pressure is checked. Blessing did not diagnose or treat; she recognised the signs and removed the delay at home.

blocks.text: After the birth

Many families relax once the baby arrives, but WHO's figures show that bleeding and infection after birth are major killers. WHO's postnatal care recommendations also include screening mothers for **depression and anxiety**. If a new mother seems unable to cope, cannot sleep even when the baby sleeps, or speaks about harming herself or the baby, she needs a health worker's help quickly. This is a health problem, not a weakness.

blocks.title: Say it simply
blocks.text: A short way to teach family members: "Bleeding, bad headache, blurred eyes, high belly pain, fever, fits: go now, day or night, with the card."

takeaways: Pre-eclampsia warning signs include severe headache, blurred vision, upper belly pain and fits.
Heavy bleeding and fever are danger signs during pregnancy and especially after birth.
When in doubt, treat a sign as danger and go to a facility.
Never give medicines or herbal mixtures instead of going.
A new mother's mental health deserves the same urgent attention.

activity.title: Make a danger sign card
steps: On a small card or phone note, list the pregnancy and after-birth danger signs from this lesson in your own words or language.
Add the name and phone number of the nearest facility that handles emergencies.
Read the card aloud to one family member and ask them to repeat the signs back to you.
Keep the card where everyone in the house can find it.
activity.evidence: A photo of your danger sign card and the name of the person you taught.

quiz.q: According to WHO, which complication is described as mostly happening after childbirth and is a leading cause of maternal death?
quiz.explain: WHO lists severe bleeding, mostly after childbirth, among the five complications that cause about 75% of maternal deaths.

quiz.q: Fatima had her first antenatal contact at 10 weeks. Which schedule matches the WHO recommendation for her remaining contacts?
options: Once a month until birth, four in total
quiz.explain: WHO recommends a first contact by 12 weeks, then contacts at 20, 26, 30, 34, 36, 38 and 40 weeks, eight in total.

quiz.q: A woman 32 weeks pregnant has a severe headache and blurred vision. What should her family do?
options: Give her a painkiller and let her sleep
Wait until her next antenatal date
Take her to a health facility immediately with her antenatal card
Ask friends on WhatsApp what they think
quiz.explain: Severe headache and visual disturbance after 20 weeks are WHO warning signs of pre-eclampsia. She needs her blood pressure checked now.

quiz.q: Her first contact was on 3 March at 11 weeks. On what date is her 20-week contact?
quiz.explain: 20 minus 11 is 9 weeks, which is 63 days. 3 March plus 63 days is 5 May.

quiz.q: Which of these is a delay at home, rather than on the road or at the facility?
options: The facility has no blood available
There is no car at night
The family waits for a husband's permission before going
quiz.explain: Waiting for permission is a delay in deciding to seek care, which happens at home. Knowledge and an agreed plan remove it.

quiz.q: A pregnant friend asks how much iron she should take. What is the right response?
options: Tell her the dose your sister used
Tell her to double it if she feels tired
Tell her the health worker decides the product and amount, and to ask at her antenatal contact
Tell her iron is not needed in pregnancy
quiz.explain: WHO recommends iron and folic acid in pregnancy, but the health worker decides what and how much. Never pass on doses.

modules.title: Birth, the Newborn Weeks and the Sick Child
modules.overview: Turn knowledge into plans: a one-page birth and emergency plan with a saving target, a postnatal check schedule with newborn danger signs, and a calm, step-by-step response when a child has diarrhoea, fever or cough.

lessons.title: The birth and emergency plan: place, people, transport and money
objectives: Choose a birth place with skilled health workers and a back-up for emergencies
Write a complete birth and emergency plan on one page
Calculate a weekly saving target for birth and transport costs
Describe the essential care every newborn should receive in the first hour

blocks.text: Labour often starts at night, on a weekend or when the person you rely on is away. Families who decide everything in advance save precious time. A **birth and emergency plan** is a short written plan that answers five questions: **where** the baby will be born, **who** will go with the mother, **how** she will get there, **how much** it will cost, and **what** to do if something goes wrong.
Why the place of birth matters

WHO stresses that **all births should be attended by skilled health professionals**, because timely management and treatment can make the difference between life and death. Its maternal mortality fact sheet notes that about 99% of births in high-income countries have a skilled attendant, compared with about 73% in low-income countries. A skilled attendant is a trained midwife, nurse or doctor who can manage a normal birth and recognise and handle complications, or refer quickly.

WHO also recommends that mother and baby receive care in the facility for **at least 24 hours after birth**. Plan for this: bring enough items for a day or more, and do not arrange to leave a few hours after the birth just to save money.

blocks.name: hospital
blocks.caption: Choose a birth place with skilled staff, and know which bigger hospital it refers emergencies to.

blocks.text: The five parts of the plan

blocks.title: One-page birth and emergency plan
items: Place and back-up facility
Companion and decision maker
Transport day and night
Money saved
Documents and bag ready
blocks.caption: If any line on the plan is blank, that is the gap to close before the last month.

head: Part of the plan
Questions to answer
Example answer
rows: Place
Where will I give birth? Where is the bigger hospital if there is an emergency?
Primary health care centre near home; general hospital for emergencies
People
Who will go with me? Who can decide to leave for the facility if my husband is away? Who cares for my other children?
Sister goes with me; sister or I can decide; neighbour minds the children
Transport
Who will drive, day and night? What is a second option?
Keke driver Musa, two numbers saved; second option a car owner on our street
Money
How much for transport, fees and supplies? How much am I saving each week?
Target about ₦25,000, saving ₦1,250 a week
Documents and bag
Where is the antenatal card? Is the bag packed by 36 weeks?
Card and bag kept by the door from week 36

blocks.title: Worked example: a weekly saving target
blocks.context: For example, Zainab is 16 weeks pregnant. She estimates a one-way trip to the general hospital at about ₦7,500 at night (approximate, prices vary by town and time). She wants money for two trips plus about ₦10,000 for other costs. She plans to finish saving by 36 weeks.
steps: Transport: 2 trips x ₦7,500 = ₦15,000.
Weeks available: 36 - 16 = 20 weeks.
Weekly target: ₦25,000 / 20 = ₦1,250 a week.
She saves it in a separate wallet on her mobile money app and tells her sister, who can reach it if needed.
blocks.result: Zainab needs to put aside ₦1,250 a week to have ₦25,000 ready by 36 weeks. If a cost is free at her facility, the saving becomes a buffer for emergencies.

blocks.title: Ask the facility, not the market
blocks.text: Ask at your antenatal contact what the facility charges and what you must bring. Some services are free or subsidised in public facilities. Use their answer, not a neighbour's guess, to set your saving target.
The first hour: essential newborn care
WHO lists essential care every newborn should receive. Knowing it helps you understand what the midwife is doing and support it:

items: **Warmth**: dry the baby and place them skin-to-skin on the mother's chest, covered with a cloth. Babies lose heat very quickly.
**Early breastfeeding**: WHO recommends starting breastfeeding **within one hour of birth**, and giving only breast milk for the first six months.
**Clean cord and skin care**: keep the cord stump clean and dry. Do not put anything on it unless a health worker tells you to.
**Checks and vaccines**: the baby is examined, and vaccines given at birth are recorded on the child's card.

blocks.title: Do not apply substances to the cord
blocks.text: Putting ash, dung, oil or any home mixture on the cord can bring infection. WHO's newborn guidance calls for hygienic cord and skin care. Follow your health worker's instructions only.
If labour starts somewhere unexpected

Even with a good plan, labour can come early or quickly. The plan still helps: the bag is ready, the drivers are saved and the money is set aside. Ask your health worker at an antenatal contact exactly when you should leave for the facility once labour begins, and leave early rather than late if the facility is far away. If a danger sign appears at any time, follow the plan for emergencies and go to the bigger hospital directly if it can be reached safely.

blocks.title: Share the plan
blocks.text: Send a photo of the plan to at least two people: the companion and the person who controls the money. A plan only one person knows is not a plan.

takeaways: A birth and emergency plan answers where, who, how, how much and what if.
WHO says all births should have a skilled attendant.
Plan for at least 24 hours of care in the facility after birth.
Divide the total cost by the weeks left to get a weekly saving target.
Skin-to-skin warmth, breastfeeding within one hour and a clean cord protect the newborn.

activity.title: Write a one-page birth plan
steps: Copy the five-part table into a notebook or phone note.
Fill every line with real names, phone numbers and places for yourself or a pregnant relative.
Ask the facility what birth costs and what to bring, then calculate the weekly saving target.
Share the finished plan with two people.
activity.evidence: A photo of the completed one-page plan with the saving calculation.

lessons.title: The six weeks after birth: postnatal checks and newborn danger signs
objectives: Schedule the WHO postnatal contacts from a baby's date of birth
Recognise the newborn danger signs that need urgent care
Explain what the mother and baby are checked for after birth
Support early, exclusive breastfeeding without giving water or other drinks

blocks.text: The weeks after birth are called the **postnatal period**. WHO's newborn fact sheet reports that most newborn deaths happen in the **first week of life**, and its maternal fact sheet shows bleeding and infection after birth are leading causes of maternal death. Yet WHO has also reported that **more than 3 in 10 women and babies do not receive postnatal care in the first days after birth**. This lesson makes sure your family is not one of them.
The WHO postnatal contacts

In 2022 WHO recommended care in a facility for **at least 24 hours after birth**, followed by **at least three more postnatal check-ups in the first six weeks**: between **48 and 72 hours**, between **7 and 14 days**, and during **week six**. These can be at the facility or through home visits, depending on what your area offers.

blocks.title: Postnatal contacts after birth
items: First 24 hours in facility
Day 2 to 3
Day 7 to 14
Week 6
blocks.caption: Four points of care in six weeks, each one a chance to catch danger early.

blocks.title: Worked example: postnatal dates from the birth date
blocks.context: For example, Chioma gave birth on Tuesday 14 July 2026. Her mother wants to know when each check is due.
steps: First 24 hours: in the facility from 14 to 15 July.
48 to 72 hours: 14 July plus 2 days is 16 July; plus 3 days is 17 July. The check is due **16 or 17 July**.
7 to 14 days: 14 July plus 7 days is 21 July; plus 14 days is 28 July. The check is due **between 21 and 28 July**.
Week six: 14 July plus 42 days is **25 August**, so the check is due in the week before that date.
They write the dates on the baby's card and in both phones.
blocks.result: The family has clear dates: 16 or 17 July, 21 to 28 July and around 25 August. If the clinic gives different dates, they follow the clinic.

blocks.text: What gets checked

head: For the mother
For the baby
rows: Bleeding, temperature and recovery from birth
Breathing, warmth, feeding and the cord
Common problems such as pain and breast engorgement
Screening for eye problems and hearing problems
Screening for depression and anxiety
Danger signs and weight
Breastfeeding support: attachment and positioning
Vaccines given at birth recorded on the card

blocks.name: breast-feeding
blocks.caption: Postnatal contacts include help with attachment and positioning so breastfeeding gets off to a good start.

blocks.text: Useful questions to ask at each postnatal check: Is my bleeding normal for this stage? Is the baby feeding and gaining weight well? Is the cord healing well? Which vaccines has the baby received, and when is the next one due? When is our next check? Write the answers on the card or in your phone so the family can see them.
Newborn danger signs
WHO advises families to seek care promptly if a newborn has any of these signs. Learn them by heart and teach them to everyone who holds the baby:

items: **Feeding problems**: the baby is not feeding well or has stopped feeding.
**Reduced activity**: the baby is unusually sleepy, floppy or moves only when stimulated, or not at all.
**Difficult breathing**.
**Fever**, or the baby **feels cold**.
**Fits or convulsions**.

blocks.title: A newborn with a danger sign goes today
blocks.text: Do not wait for the next scheduled check. Keep the baby warm against the mother's skin, keep offering the breast if the baby can feed, and go to a facility immediately with the baby's card. Do not give herbal mixtures, glucose water or medicines on the way.
Breastfeeding: the basics that matter here

WHO recommends that babies start breastfeeding **within one hour of birth**, receive **only breast milk for the first six months** (no water, no glucose water, no herbal drinks, no formula unless a health worker advises it), and continue breastfeeding **up to two years or beyond**. In the postnatal period, the most useful thing a family can do is protect the mother's time and rest so she can feed often, and bring her to the checks where health workers help with attachment and positioning. Our companion course on community nutrition covers feeding from six months onwards in detail.

blocks.title: Tradition and the first milk
blocks.text: The thick yellowish first milk is part of breast milk and is good for the baby. If relatives suggest throwing it away or giving water first, kindly explain that WHO recommends breast milk only, starting in the first hour.
The mother after birth

Families often focus on the baby and forget the mother. Remember the danger signs from Module 1: heavy bleeding, fever, severe headache, fits. Add her mood. WHO now includes screening for postnatal depression and anxiety. A mother who feels hopeless, cannot sleep even when she can, or cannot care for herself or the baby should be taken to a health worker. Practical help, such as cooking, washing and taking turns with the baby at night, protects her recovery.

blocks.title: Ask about family planning
blocks.text: The postnatal contacts are a good time to ask a health worker about family planning options that are suitable while breastfeeding, so the next pregnancy comes when the family is ready.

takeaways: WHO recommends at least 24 hours of facility care after birth and three more checks in six weeks.
Checks fall at 48 to 72 hours, 7 to 14 days and week six.
Newborn danger signs: feeding problems, reduced activity, difficult breathing, fever or feeling cold, fits.
Only breast milk for six months, starting within one hour of birth.
Watch the mother too: bleeding, fever, headache and her mood.

activity.title: Postnatal date card
steps: Pick a real or example birth date.
Calculate the three postnatal check dates and write them down.
Write the five newborn danger signs on the same card.
Explain the card to the person who will help the mother after birth.
activity.evidence: A photo of the date card with the danger signs and the name of the helper you explained it to.

lessons.title: When a child is sick: diarrhoea, fever and cough
objectives: Recognise the general danger signs that mean a sick child must go now
Identify signs of dehydration and explain how ORS works
Explain why a child with fever in a malaria area should be tested before treatment
Recognise the breathing signs of pneumonia

blocks.text: Young children get sick often, and most illnesses get better. The skill you need is to tell the difference between a child you can care for at home **while staying in touch with a health worker**, and a child who must go to a facility **now**. This lesson covers three common problems: diarrhoea, fever and cough. It does not teach treatment with medicines; those decisions belong to a health worker.
Signs that mean go now

Whatever the illness, take a child to a facility immediately if the child: **cannot drink or breastfeed**, **has fits (convulsions)**, is **very sleepy, floppy or cannot be woken**, or is **breathing fast or with the chest pulling in**. WHO lists these among the signs of severe pneumonia and severe dehydration, and they are dangerous whatever the cause.

blocks.name: face-with-thermometer
blocks.alt: A face with a thermometer in its mouth
blocks.caption: Fever is common in children, but some signs alongside it mean the child must go now.

blocks.text: Diarrhoea and dehydration

WHO defines diarrhoea as **three or more loose or watery stools in a day**, or more often than is normal for that person. The danger is **dehydration**: the body loses water and salts faster than they are replaced. WHO describes two levels:

head: Level
Signs WHO describes
What to do
rows: Some dehydration
Restless or irritable, sunken eyes, drinks eagerly, thirsty
Start ORS and go to a health worker for assessment
Severe dehydration
Very sleepy or unconscious, sunken eyes, unable to drink or drinks poorly, skin pinch goes back very slowly (2 seconds or more)
Emergency: go to a facility now

blocks.text: **Oral rehydration solution (ORS)** is, in WHO's words, a mixture of clean water, salt and sugar. It replaces what diarrhoea removes and costs very little. Buy ORS sachets from a pharmacy or get them at your clinic, and mix each sachet **exactly as the packet says, with clean water**. Using the wrong amount of water can make the drink unsafe or weak. Ask the health worker how much to give your child. WHO also notes that **zinc**, given by a health worker, shortens diarrhoea episodes.

items: Keep breastfeeding, and breastfeed more often. WHO advises more fluids and more frequent breastfeeding during illness.
Keep offering soft, favourite foods to older babies and children.
Go to a health worker if there is **blood in the stool**, if diarrhoea **goes on for many days**, or if you see signs of dehydration.

blocks.title: Worked example: keeping a diarrhoea log
blocks.context: For example, Aisha's son Sani is 14 months old. He has loose stools from Saturday morning. Aisha writes each one down with the time.
steps: By 2 pm she has recorded 3 loose stools: 7 am, 10 am and 1:30 pm. By WHO's definition this is diarrhoea.
She has ORS sachets at home from the clinic. She mixes one exactly as the packet says, in clean water, and offers it in small sips from a cup, while continuing to breastfeed.
At 6 pm she checks for danger signs: Sani is alert, drinks eagerly, no blood in the stool, no sunken eyes.
By 9 pm the count is 6 loose stools in the day. On Sunday morning he is restless and his eyes look sunken.
Restless with sunken eyes are signs of dehydration, so she takes him to the clinic that morning, with the log and his card.
blocks.result: Aisha did not wait for the illness to become severe. Her written log (6 stools in about 14 hours) let the health worker understand the illness quickly.

blocks.text: Fever and malaria

WHO's malaria fact sheet lists fever, headache and chills as the most common early symptoms, usually starting 10 to 15 days after an infected mosquito bite. Children under five and pregnant women are among those at highest risk. WHO recommends that **every suspected case of malaria is confirmed with a test**, either a rapid diagnostic test (RDT) or microscopy, **before treatment**. Many fevers are not malaria, so buying malaria medicine without a test can miss the real illness.

blocks.title: Test, do not guess
blocks.text: Take a child with fever to a health worker or facility for a malaria test. Do not buy and give antimalarials or antibiotics on your own, and never use leftover medicine from another child.
Cough and fast breathing

WHO's pneumonia fact sheet explains that a child with cough or difficult breathing who has **fast breathing or lower chest wall indrawing** (the lower chest sucks in when the child breathes in) may have pneumonia. Pneumonia needs antibiotics chosen and given by a health worker. Severe cases may show inability to feed or drink, unconsciousness, a low body temperature or fits.

blocks.title: Sick child at home: what to do
items: Look for go-now signs
None: home care and see health worker
Any go-now sign: leave now
Bring card and notes
blocks.caption: Check for go-now signs first, every time, before deciding on home care.

blocks.title: Notes help the health worker
blocks.text: Write down when the illness started, the number of stools, the fevers you noticed and what the child has drunk and eaten. Bring the child's card. Clear notes save time at the facility.

takeaways: Cannot drink or breastfeed, fits, very sleepy or floppy, fast or difficult breathing: go now.
Diarrhoea is three or more loose stools a day; dehydration is the danger.
Mix ORS exactly as the packet says and keep breastfeeding.
WHO recommends testing for malaria before treatment.
Medicines for children come from a health worker, not from guesswork.

activity.title: Prepare a sick-child kit
steps: Find out where you can get ORS sachets nearby and buy or collect two.
Read the mixing instructions on the packet and note the amount of clean water needed.
Write the go-now signs on a card and keep it with the ORS and the child's health card.
Show the kit to another caregiver in your home.
activity.evidence: A photo of your kit: ORS sachets, go-now card and the child's health card.

quiz.q: Zainab needs ₦25,000 for birth costs and has 20 weeks left to save. What is her weekly saving target?
quiz.explain: ₦25,000 divided by 20 weeks is ₦1,250 a week.

quiz.q: A baby was born on 14 July. When is the WHO postnatal check that falls 48 to 72 hours after birth?
quiz.explain: 14 July plus 2 days is 16 July, plus 3 days is 17 July.

quiz.q: A 5-day-old baby has stopped feeding and feels cold. What should the family do?
options: Give a herbal drink to warm the baby
Wait for the 7 to 14 day check
Keep the baby warm skin-to-skin and go to a facility now
quiz.explain: Feeding problems and feeling cold are WHO newborn danger signs. The baby needs a health worker today.

quiz.q: A 1-year-old with diarrhoea is very sleepy, has sunken eyes and cannot drink. What does this suggest?
options: Some dehydration only, safe to wait a day
quiz.explain: Lethargy, sunken eyes and being unable to drink are WHO signs of severe dehydration. Go to a facility now.

quiz.q: A child has a fever. What does WHO recommend before malaria treatment?
options: A malaria test, such as a rapid diagnostic test
Give leftover medicine from a sibling
quiz.explain: WHO recommends confirming suspected malaria with a test before treatment, because many fevers are not malaria.

quiz.q: How should ORS from a sachet be prepared?
options: With extra sugar to make it sweeter
With half the water to make it stronger
With soft drink instead of water
Exactly as the packet says, with clean water
quiz.explain: The wrong amount of water makes ORS harmful or weak. Follow the packet and use clean water.

quiz.q: Which newborn care practice does WHO recommend straight after birth?
options: Bathing the baby immediately in cold water
Skin-to-skin contact and breastfeeding within one hour
Giving water before the first breastfeed
Applying oil and ash to the cord
quiz.explain: WHO's essential newborn care includes warmth through skin-to-skin contact and early breastfeeding within one hour.

modules.title: Prevention, Community Sharing and Your Action Plan
modules.overview: Build the everyday prevention habits that protect children, learn to share health information accurately and kindly, and bring the whole course together into a family health action plan with a 90-day outreach plan you can measure.

lessons.title: Prevention habits that protect children: vaccines, nets and clean hands
objectives: Explain which serious childhood illnesses vaccines help prevent
Keep a child's vaccination card up to date and never miss a due date
Use mosquito nets, handwashing and clean air habits every day
Score your household's prevention habits and choose one to improve

blocks.text: Module 2 was about what to do when danger appears. This lesson is about stopping illness before it starts. Prevention is quiet work: no single day feels dramatic, but the habits add up. WHO's fact sheets on pneumonia, diarrhoea and malaria all point to the same small set of habits: **vaccines, mosquito nets, handwashing with soap, safe water, breastfeeding and clean air at home**.
Vaccines: the strongest single habit

WHO's pneumonia fact sheet calls immunisation against **Hib, pneumococcus, measles and whooping cough (pertussis)** the most effective way to prevent pneumonia. Its diarrhoea fact sheet lists **rotavirus vaccination** as a prevention measure. For malaria, WHO has recommended two vaccines for children living in areas with moderate to high malaria transmission: **RTS,S/AS01** (since 2021) and **R21/Matrix-M** (since 2023). In pregnancy, WHO recommends **tetanus vaccination** for all pregnant women to protect the newborn.

Each vaccine is given at a set age, and many need more than one dose to protect fully. The schedule is set by the national programme, and it can change as new vaccines are introduced. So the most reliable guide for your child is not a poster or a WhatsApp message but **the child's own vaccination card**, filled in by the health worker.

blocks.name: syringe
blocks.caption: Each dose on the card is a step towards full protection; a missed dose leaves a gap.

blocks.title: The vaccination card habit
items: Go on the due date
Health worker records dose
Write next date
Set phone reminder
blocks.caption: Repeat the cycle at every visit until the card is complete.

items: Bring the card to every clinic visit, including visits for illness.
After each dose, check that it was written on the card and ask: When is the next one?
Save the next date in your phone with a reminder two days before.
If a date is missed, go to the clinic as soon as possible and ask how to catch up. Do not wait for a campaign.
Keep the card in a plastic sleeve, and take a clear photo of it in case it is lost.

blocks.text: Mosquito nets

WHO advises sleeping under a mosquito net in places where malaria is present. Children under five and pregnant women are among those most at risk. A net only works if it is used every night, all year, and tucked in well. Check nets for holes, and make sure the people most at risk, the pregnant woman and the youngest children, sleep under one first. In pregnancy, malaria prevention also includes the preventive treatment offered at antenatal care.

Treat the net as protective equipment, not bedding. Hang it so it reaches the floor or can be tucked under the mattress or mat, repair small holes quickly with needle and thread, and keep it away from candles and cooking fires.
Clean hands, safe water, clean air

WHO's diarrhoea fact sheet lists safe drinking water, improved sanitation, **handwashing with soap**, exclusive breastfeeding for the first six months, good personal and food hygiene, and health education. The pneumonia fact sheet adds **reducing indoor air pollution** and good hygiene in crowded homes. Smoke from cooking with firewood or charcoal inside a closed room is a form of indoor air pollution, so cook in a well ventilated place and keep babies away from the smoke.

items: Wash hands with soap and water before preparing food, before feeding a child, and after using the toilet or cleaning a child's bottom.
Store drinking water covered, and pour it out rather than dipping cups into it.
Use a toilet or latrine, and dispose of children's stools safely.

blocks.title: Worked example: a household prevention score
blocks.context: For example, Funmi uses an 8-point checklist to score her home, giving 1 point for each habit fully in place.
steps: Vaccination cards up to date for both children: yes, 1 point.
Everyone at highest risk sleeps under a net every night: no, her toddler often sleeps outside the net, 0 points.
Soap and water at the handwashing spot every day: yes, 1 point.
Drinking water stored covered: yes, 1 point. Toilet used by all: yes, 1 point.
Cooking smoke kept away from the children: no, she cooks indoors with charcoal, 0 points.
Card photos saved on her phone: yes, 1 point. ORS sachets at home: yes, 1 point.
blocks.result: Funmi scores 6 out of 8. She chooses one change for this month: moving her toddler's sleeping mat inside the net. Next month she will move the charcoal stove to the open veranda.

blocks.title: One habit at a time
blocks.text: Do not try to fix everything at once. Choose the habit with the biggest risk, make it automatic for a month, then choose the next.

blocks.title: Vaccine questions
blocks.text: If you or a family member has doubts about a vaccine, write the question down and ask a health worker at the clinic. They can explain what the vaccine protects against and what reactions to expect.

takeaways: Vaccines are the strongest single way to prevent pneumonia and several other killers.
The child's card, not rumours, is the guide to which dose is due next.
If a dose is missed, go to the clinic and ask how to catch up.
Nets every night, handwashing with soap, safe water and smoke-free air protect children.
Improve one habit at a time and track your score.

activity.title: Score your home
steps: Copy the 8-point checklist from the worked example.
Score your own home honestly, 1 point per habit fully in place.
Choose one habit to improve this month and write what you will do.
Photograph each child's vaccination card and save the next due date in your phone.
activity.evidence: Your scored checklist, the habit you chose, and a saved card photo with the next due date.

lessons.title: Sharing health information responsibly: myths, WhatsApp and the health team
objectives: Check a health message against a reliable source before sharing it
Respond kindly to common myths about pregnancy, newborns and sick children
Work alongside community health workers and clinics rather than replacing them
Protect privacy when talking or posting about someone's health

blocks.text: After this course, people may start asking you health questions. That is a privilege and a responsibility. Good health information can save a life; wrong information, even when shared with love, can delay care. This lesson is about how to share well: check first, speak simply, point people to health workers and protect privacy.
Check before you forward
Health messages spread fast on WhatsApp, often with no source. Before you forward or repeat one, run it through four questions:

blocks.title: Check a health message
items: Who says so?
Does WHO or a clinic agree?
Does it delay care?
Share, correct or delete
blocks.caption: If a message cannot pass the first two checks, do not forward it.

items: **Who says so?** A named health organisation, such as WHO or the Federal Ministry of Health, or a health worker you know? Or an unnamed forward?
**Does a reliable source agree?** Look for the same advice on an official site, or ask at your clinic.
**Could it delay care?** Any message that says to treat danger signs at home, or to avoid the clinic, is dangerous.
**Then decide**: share it with the source, correct it kindly, or delete it.

blocks.name: sharing-knowledge
blocks.caption: Share what you have checked, and always point people back to a health worker.

blocks.text: Common beliefs and what WHO says

head: What people sometimes say
What WHO guidance says
A kind way to respond
rows: Give the newborn water in hot weather
Only breast milk for the first six months, no water
Breast milk already contains the water a baby needs; feed more often in the heat.
Every fever is malaria, just buy medicine
Confirm suspected malaria with a test before treatment
Let us get a quick test at the clinic so we treat the right illness.
Four antenatal visits are enough
At least eight contacts, the first by 12 weeks
The new advice is eight contacts; each one checks blood pressure and the baby.
Rub something on the cord to dry it
Hygienic cord care; keep it clean and dry
Clean and dry is best. The nurse will say if anything is needed.
Stop breastfeeding when the baby has diarrhoea
Breastfeed more often during illness
Keep breastfeeding; it helps the baby recover.

blocks.title: Respect, not argument
blocks.text: Older relatives often hold these beliefs out of love and experience. Thank them, explain the reason simply, and suggest asking the health worker together. People change more easily when they do not feel ashamed.
Working with the health team

In Nigeria, primary health care centres are often the first point of care, and **community health extension workers (CHEWs)** and other community health workers visit homes, give health education and refer people to facilities. Get to know the health workers who serve your area. Ask them what days antenatal care and immunisation run, how to reach them in an emergency and how you can help, for example by reminding mothers of vaccination dates. You support their work; you do not replace it.

blocks.title: Worked example: answering a WhatsApp forward
blocks.context: For example, a message arrives in Grace's church women's group: "Pregnant women should drink this herbal mixture every morning to prevent all complications. Forward to 10 women."
steps: Who says so? No name, no organisation. First check failed.

Does WHO agree? WHO's antenatal guidance relies on contacts with a health worker, blood pressure checks and supplements the health worker gives. It does not say any mixture prevents all complications.
Could it delay care? Yes. A woman who trusts the mixture might ignore a headache or bleeding.

Grace replies kindly in the group: "Thank you for caring. I could not find this advice from WHO or our clinic. The safest protection is the eight antenatal contacts and going straight to the hospital with any danger sign. Please ask the nurse before taking any mixture in pregnancy."
blocks.result: Grace stopped the message spreading in her group without shaming the sender, and gave a clear, checked alternative.

blocks.text: Speaking simply

items: Use the words people use at home, in their own language, and explain any medical word once, for example: pre-eclampsia means dangerous high blood pressure in pregnancy.
Teach a few signs at a time, and ask the person to say them back to you.
Say what to do, not only what to fear: which facility, how to get there, what to bring.
Use pictures or your danger sign card for people who do not read easily.

blocks.text: Privacy and consent

Health information is personal. Do not share someone's pregnancy, illness, test results or photos without their permission, even in a prayer request. When you teach, use examples without names. If someone tells you something private, keep it private, unless their life is in danger and you need to get them help.

blocks.title: Know your limits
blocks.text: If someone asks which medicine to take or how much, the answer is always: ask the health worker or pharmacist who can examine you. Saying "I do not know, let us ask the nurse" is a strength, not a weakness.

takeaways: Check who said it, whether a reliable source agrees, and whether it could delay care.
Correct myths kindly and explain the reason.
Community health workers and clinics are your partners; support, never replace them.
Never answer medicine or dose questions; refer to a health worker.
Keep other people's health information private.

activity.title: Myth check
steps: Find one health message about pregnancy, babies or child illness that you have received or heard.
Run it through the four checks and write your answers.
Write a short, kind reply that you could send or say.
Find the name and phone number of a health worker or community health worker serving your area.
activity.evidence: Your four-check notes, your written reply, and the health worker's name and contact.

lessons.title: Your family health action plan and 90-day outreach
objectives: Map the health facilities and services you can actually reach
Combine danger signs, plans and contacts into one family health action plan
Set realistic 90-day outreach targets and track them
Review and update your plan as your family's situation changes

blocks.text: This lesson brings everything together into one document: your **family health action plan**. It is the capstone of the course. It should fit on two or three pages, use real names, places and numbers, and be something your family can pick up in an emergency and follow.
Part 1: your facility map
A plan is only as good as the facilities behind it. Visit or call your nearest facilities and record what they actually offer, not what you assume.

head: Question
Facility A (nearest)
Facility B (emergency back-up)
rows: Name and address
Write the real name
Write the real name
Travel time day and night, and how
Example: 10 minutes on foot
Example: 40 minutes by car
Antenatal care and immunisation days
Ask at reception
Ask at reception
Births: skilled staff present? Open at night?
Ask
Ask
Can it handle emergencies such as heavy bleeding?
Ask
Ask
Phone number and contact person
Save in phone
Save in phone

blocks.name: route-planning
blocks.alt: A person planning a route on a map
blocks.caption: Knowing the real route, time and services of each facility removes delays before they happen.

blocks.text: Part 2: danger signs and personal plan

items: The pregnancy and after-birth danger signs (Module 1, Lesson 3).
The newborn danger signs (Module 2, Lesson 2).
The go-now signs for a sick child (Module 2, Lesson 3).
Your birth and emergency plan, or your sick-child plan if no one is pregnant: who decides, who drives, where the money is, where the cards are.

blocks.text: Part 3: a 90-day outreach plan

Health literacy spreads person to person. A good outreach plan is small and specific: **who** you will teach, **what** you will teach, **when**, and **how you will know it worked**. Choose people who most need the information: a pregnant relative, a first-time mother, a grandmother who minds children, a husband or brother who controls transport money.

blocks.title: A 90-day outreach plan
items: Days 1 to 30: household
Days 31 to 60: relatives and neighbours
Days 61 to 90: group session
Day 90: review
blocks.caption: Start close to home, widen gradually, then review and plan the next 90 days.

blocks.title: Worked example: setting and tracking targets
blocks.context: For example, Kemi plans her 90 days. Her household has 4 adults. She also has 6 relatives and neighbours with young children or pregnancies, and her women's group of 15 meets monthly.
steps: Days 1 to 30: teach all 4 adults at home the danger sign card. Target: 4 people.
Days 31 to 60: visit the 6 relatives and neighbours, 2 per week for 3 weeks. Target: 6 people.
Days 61 to 90: one 20-minute session at the women's group, if the leader agrees. Target: 15 people.
Total target: 4 + 6 + 15 = 25 people.
Check: after each conversation, ask the person to name three danger signs. Count it as success only if they can.
At day 90 she has reached 21 people, and 18 could name three signs. 18 / 21 is about 86%.
blocks.result: Kemi reached 21 of her 25 target, and about 86% of them could name three danger signs. She notes that two neighbours travelled, and adds them to the next 90-day plan.

blocks.title: Stay within your role
blocks.text: In outreach you share danger signs, plans and where to get care. You do not examine, diagnose, sell medicines or advise doses. Invite a community health worker to your group session if you can.
Part 4: the first ten minutes of an emergency

Put a short emergency script at the very top of your plan. In a real emergency people panic and forget long documents, so the first page should tell anyone in the house exactly what to do, in order, in a few lines.

items: Recognise: is this a danger sign on our list? If unsure, treat it as one.
Call the driver on the plan; if there is no answer within a few minutes, call the second number.
Call the facility to say you are coming and what the problem is.
Pick up the bag, the antenatal or child health card, the phone and charger, and the money.
Go to the facility that can handle emergencies, with the companion named in the plan.

blocks.text: Practise the script once with your household, like a fire drill. Time how long it takes to call the driver, gather the card and money and be at the door. If it takes too long, find out why: perhaps the card is in a drawer nobody can open, or the money is with someone who is away. Fix it now, while there is no emergency.
Part 5: a simple tracking sheet

head: Date
Who (no full names needed)
What I taught
Could they name three signs?
rows: Example: 4 May
Sister-in-law, pregnant
Pregnancy danger signs and birth plan
Yes
Example: 11 May
Neighbour, mother of a baby
Newborn danger signs and postnatal dates
Not yet, revisit next week

blocks.text: Keeping the plan alive

items: Keep a printed or written copy by the door and a photo in two phones.
Review it whenever something changes: a new pregnancy, a new baby, a move, a new phone number.
Check vaccination due dates on each child's card at the start of every month.
Update your facility map once a year, or sooner if a facility changes its hours or services.
Repeat the danger signs at family meetings so that everyone, including older children, knows them.

blocks.title: A reminder
blocks.text: This course does not replace care from a health worker. Your action plan is a bridge to that care: it helps your family recognise danger early and reach skilled help without delay.

takeaways: Record what facilities really offer, including night services and emergency care.
Your action plan joins danger signs, a personal plan and a facility map.
Outreach targets should name who, what, when and how you will check understanding.
Measure success by whether people can name the danger signs, not only by how many you talked to.
Review the plan whenever family circumstances change.

activity.title: Draft your action plan
steps: Complete the facility map for two facilities by visiting or calling them.
Collect your danger sign card, birth or sick-child plan and contacts into one document.
Write a 90-day outreach plan with names or groups, dates and a numeric target.
Ask one family member to read the plan and tell you what they would do if a danger sign appeared.
activity.evidence: The draft action plan with the completed facility map and the 90-day targets.

quiz.q: According to WHO, what is the most effective way to prevent pneumonia in children?
options: Immunisation against Hib, pneumococcus, measles and whooping cough
quiz.explain: WHO's pneumonia fact sheet names immunisation against these four as the most effective prevention.

quiz.q: A mother realises her child missed a vaccine dose two weeks ago. What should she do?
options: Wait for the next national campaign
Start the whole schedule again from birth
Go to the clinic as soon as possible with the card and ask how to catch up
quiz.explain: Going promptly with the card lets the health worker decide how to catch up. Waiting leaves the child unprotected.

quiz.q: Funmi scores 1, 0, 1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 1 on her 8 prevention habits. What is her score?
A WhatsApp forward with no source says a mixture prevents all pregnancy complications. What is the best response?
options: Forward it to 10 women as asked
Reply kindly that you could not confirm it, and point to antenatal contacts and danger signs
Try the mixture first to see
quiz.explain: The message fails the source check and could delay care. A kind correction with checked advice protects the group.

quiz.q: Kemi reached 21 people and 18 could name three danger signs. About what percentage is that?
quiz.explain: 18 divided by 21 is about 0.857, or about 86%.

quiz.q: During outreach, a neighbour asks how many tablets of a medicine to give her child. What should you say?
options: Tell her the number you used for your child
Say you are not able to advise doses and help her reach a health worker or pharmacist
Guess based on the child's age
Tell her to give half of an adult dose
quiz.explain: Dose advice belongs to health workers. Your role is to help her reach one quickly.

quiz.q: Which of these is a WHO-listed way to prevent childhood diarrhoea?
quiz.explain: WHO lists handwashing with soap, safe water, sanitation, exclusive breastfeeding for six months and rotavirus vaccination among prevention measures.

finalQuiz.q: About what share of maternal deaths does WHO link to five complications such as severe bleeding, infection and pre-eclampsia?
finalQuiz.explain: WHO's maternal mortality fact sheet says these five complications account for about 75% of maternal deaths.

finalQuiz.q: When should the first antenatal contact happen, according to WHO?
finalQuiz.explain: WHO recommends the first contact in the first 12 weeks, followed by contacts at 20, 26, 30, 34, 36, 38 and 40 weeks.

finalQuiz.q: Which group of signs after 20 weeks of pregnancy can point to pre-eclampsia?
options: Severe headache, blurred vision and upper belly pain
finalQuiz.explain: WHO lists severe headache, visual disturbances and upper abdominal pain among the warning signs of pre-eclampsia.

finalQuiz.q: Three days after giving birth at home, a woman has a fever and feels very unwell. What should happen?
options: She rests and drinks herbal tea
She waits for the six-week check
She goes to a health facility immediately
finalQuiz.explain: Infection after childbirth is a major cause of maternal death. Fever after birth is a danger sign.

finalQuiz.q: Birth costs are estimated at ₦30,000 and there are 15 weeks left to save. What is the weekly target?
finalQuiz.explain: ₦30,000 divided by 15 weeks is ₦2,000 a week.

finalQuiz.q: How long does WHO recommend that mother and baby receive care in a facility after birth?
finalQuiz.explain: WHO's 2022 postnatal recommendations call for care in the facility for at least 24 hours after birth.

finalQuiz.q: Which is a WHO newborn danger sign?
finalQuiz.explain: WHO lists feeding problems, reduced activity, difficult breathing, fever, fits and feeling cold as newborn danger signs.

finalQuiz.q: A 2-year-old has had 4 loose stools today, is alert and drinking well. What is the best next step?
options: Give ORS mixed exactly as the packet says, keep feeding, watch for danger signs and see a health worker
finalQuiz.explain: Three or more loose stools a day is diarrhoea. ORS, continued feeding and contact with a health worker are right, going immediately if danger signs appear.

finalQuiz.q: A child with a cough is breathing fast and the lower chest pulls in with each breath. What does this suggest?
options: Possible pneumonia: go to a health worker now
A normal cold, no action needed
finalQuiz.explain: WHO describes fast breathing or lower chest wall indrawing in a child with cough as signs of pneumonia, which needs a health worker's treatment.

finalQuiz.q: Which pair of malaria vaccines has WHO recommended for children in moderate to high transmission areas?
finalQuiz.explain: WHO recommended RTS,S/AS01 in 2021 and R21/Matrix-M in 2023 for children in these areas.

finalQuiz.q: A relative insists a newborn needs water in the hot season. What is the WHO-based response?
options: Agree and give a little water
Explain that WHO recommends only breast milk for six months, and suggest feeding more often
finalQuiz.explain: WHO recommends exclusive breastfeeding, no water, for the first six months.

finalQuiz.q: Which outreach measure best shows that your teaching worked?
options: How many WhatsApp messages you sent
Whether people can name three danger signs afterwards
How many people liked your post
finalQuiz.explain: Checking that people can name the danger signs tests real understanding, the goal of health literacy.

capstone.title: Maternal and Child Health Action Plan
capstone.brief: A two to three page family health action plan: your written danger sign lists with a personal care-seeking plan, a map of the facilities and community health workers you can really reach, and a 90-day plan to share this knowledge with family and community contacts.
steps: List the pregnancy, after-birth, newborn and sick-child danger signs in your own words or language.
Write your care-seeking plan: who decides, who drives (two numbers), where the money is and where the cards are kept.
Visit or call two facilities and complete the facility map, including night and emergency services; add a community health worker's contact.
Write a 90-day outreach plan with named people or groups, dates and numeric targets.
Carry it out, record how many people you reached and how many could name three danger signs.
Review the plan at day 90 and update it for the next 90 days.
evidence: Danger sign lists for all four groups
Care-seeking plan with names, phone numbers and money arrangement
Facility map for two facilities plus a community health worker contact
Statement that the plan supports, and does not replace, care from health workers
